people.name: Kenji Varela

paragraphs.text: For most of recorded history, loading a ship looked much the same. Goods arrived at the quayside in sacks, barrels, bales and crates of every shape, and gangs of dockworkers carried, rolled or hoisted each item aboard, fitting it into the hold by hand. A single cargo ship in the early 1950s might hold tens of thousands of separate items, and loading or unloading it could take a week or more. Vessels often spent as many days tied up in port as they did at sea. The process was also costly in other ways: cargo was damaged by careless handling, and a share of it routinely disappeared into workers' pockets or onto passing lorries. For many goods, the expense of moving them across a few hundred metres of dock was a large fraction of the cost of the entire journey.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The notion of packing cargo into large, reusable boxes was not new. Railways in several countries had experimented with removable freight boxes in the early twentieth century, and some shipping lines used small steel crates, but these schemes stayed local and never spread widely. The decisive step came in 1956, when an American entrepreneur who had built his fortune running a trucking business bought a shipping company and had an old tanker converted to carry 58 detachable trailer bodies. It sailed from Newark to Houston, and the cost of loading it was a small fraction of the usual rate. What made the experiment important was not the box itself but the thinking behind it: the entrepreneur saw that the real business was not operating ships but moving goods, and that the ship was simply one link in a chain that also included lorries, trains and warehouses.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: For the idea to work on a global scale, however, the boxes had to be identical. In the early years each company built containers to its own design, in lengths that varied from firm to firm, and a box belonging to one firm could not be lifted by another firm's cranes or fitted into its ships. Through the 1960s, engineers, manufacturers and government officials negotiated a common standard, and the International Organization for Standardization eventually settled on lengths of 20 and 40 feet, together with a uniform width and a strong steel fitting at each corner. These corner fittings, locked together with a simple twisting device, allow containers to be stacked many layers high and fastened securely to ships, rail wagons and lorry trailers. Standardisation also produced a new unit of measurement, the twenty-foot equivalent unit, or TEU. Above all, it meant that goods could be sealed inside a box at a factory and not handled again until they reached their final destination.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The new system transformed the geography of ports. A container terminal needs deep water for large ships, giant cranes and, above all, vast areas of flat land on which thousands of boxes can be stacked and sorted. Old harbours in the hearts of cities, squeezed between narrow streets and ageing warehouses, had no room to expand, and trade moved to new sites. In New York, activity drained away from the piers of Manhattan and Brooklyn towards spacious terminals across the harbour in New Jersey; in Britain, London's historic docks closed one after another while the small port of Felixstowe grew into the country's busiest container port. The human cost was severe. The economic historian Wilhelmina Oduya, in her study of three European ports, found that dock employment fell by roughly two-thirds within fifteen years of each port opening its first container terminal.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Ships changed just as dramatically. The first purpose-built container ships carried a few hundred boxes; the largest vessels today carry more than 20,000 TEU. Because cranes can move a container every minute or two, a ship that once spent a week in port may now be turned around in a matter of hours. Lower costs per box encouraged shipping lines to build ever bigger vessels and to merge into a handful of giant companies. Yet the port economist Kenji Varela argues that the most important gain was not cheapness but predictability. When manufacturers could be confident that a consignment would arrive on a given day, he says, they could reduce the stocks they held in reserve and spread production across several countries, assembling products from parts made thousands of kilometres apart.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Economists still debate how much of the growth in world trade since the 1960s can be credited to the container, but some have argued that its effect was greater than that of many trade agreements. Its success has also created new weaknesses. Because global supply chains depend on boxes arriving exactly when expected, a single blocked canal or a shortage of empty containers can delay deliveries around the world for months. And because a sealed steel box looks the same whatever it holds, customs authorities can physically inspect only a small proportion of those passing through their ports, which makes the system attractive to smugglers. The plain metal container remains one of the least noticed inventions of the twentieth century, but few objects have done more to shape the world economy.
paragraphs.label: F

section.text:
The Box That Changed Trade

A. For most of recorded history, loading a ship looked much the same. Goods arrived at the quayside in sacks, barrels, bales and crates of every shape, and gangs of dockworkers carried, rolled or hoisted each item aboard, fitting it into the hold by hand. A single cargo ship in the early 1950s might hold tens of thousands of separate items, and loading or unloading it could take a week or more. Vessels often spent as many days tied up in port as they did at sea. The process was also costly in other ways: cargo was damaged by careless handling, and a share of it routinely disappeared into workers' pockets or onto passing lorries. For many goods, the expense of moving them across a few hundred metres of dock was a large fraction of the cost of the entire journey.

B. The notion of packing cargo into large, reusable boxes was not new. Railways in several countries had experimented with removable freight boxes in the early twentieth century, and some shipping lines used small steel crates, but these schemes stayed local and never spread widely. The decisive step came in 1956, when an American entrepreneur who had built his fortune running a trucking business bought a shipping company and had an old tanker converted to carry 58 detachable trailer bodies. It sailed from Newark to Houston, and the cost of loading it was a small fraction of the usual rate. What made the experiment important was not the box itself but the thinking behind it: the entrepreneur saw that the real business was not operating ships but moving goods, and that the ship was simply one link in a chain that also included lorries, trains and warehouses.

C. For the idea to work on a global scale, however, the boxes had to be identical. In the early years each company built containers to its own design, in lengths that varied from firm to firm, and a box belonging to one firm could not be lifted by another firm's cranes or fitted into its ships. Through the 1960s, engineers, manufacturers and government officials negotiated a common standard, and the International Organization for Standardization eventually settled on lengths of 20 and 40 feet, together with a uniform width and a strong steel fitting at each corner. These corner fittings, locked together with a simple twisting device, allow containers to be stacked many layers high and fastened securely to ships, rail wagons and lorry trailers. Standardisation also produced a new unit of measurement, the twenty-foot equivalent unit, or TEU. Above all, it meant that goods could be sealed inside a box at a factory and not handled again until they reached their final destination.

D. The new system transformed the geography of ports. A container terminal needs deep water for large ships, giant cranes and, above all, vast areas of flat land on which thousands of boxes can be stacked and sorted. Old harbours in the hearts of cities, squeezed between narrow streets and ageing warehouses, had no room to expand, and trade moved to new sites. In New York, activity drained away from the piers of Manhattan and Brooklyn towards spacious terminals across the harbour in New Jersey; in Britain, London's historic docks closed one after another while the small port of Felixstowe grew into the country's busiest container port. The human cost was severe. The economic historian Wilhelmina Oduya, in her study of three European ports, found that dock employment fell by roughly two-thirds within fifteen years of each port opening its first container terminal.

E. Ships changed just as dramatically. The first purpose-built container ships carried a few hundred boxes; the largest vessels today carry more than 20,000 TEU. Because cranes can move a container every minute or two, a ship that once spent a week in port may now be turned around in a matter of hours. Lower costs per box encouraged shipping lines to build ever bigger vessels and to merge into a handful of giant companies. Yet the port economist Kenji Varela argues that the most important gain was not cheapness but predictability. When manufacturers could be confident that a consignment would arrive on a given day, he says, they could reduce the stocks they held in reserve and spread production across several countries, assembling products from parts made thousands of kilometres apart.

F. Economists still debate how much of the growth in world trade since the 1960s can be credited to the container, but some have argued that its effect was greater than that of many trade agreements. Its success has also created new weaknesses. Because global supply chains depend on boxes arriving exactly when expected, a single blocked canal or a shortage of empty containers can delay deliveries around the world for months. And because a sealed steel box looks the same whatever it holds, customs authorities can physically inspect only a small proportion of those passing through their ports, which makes the system attractive to smugglers. The plain metal container remains one of the least noticed inventions of the twentieth century, but few objects have done more to shape the world economy.
